book.unit_title: Major geological processes associated with plate tectonics

title: Plate movements and plate boundaries
competency: Describe convergent, divergent and transform boundaries, their landforms, and what drives the plates.

keywords.def: Plates move toward each other; the denser plate is subducted and destroyed (destructive).
Plates move apart; rising magma makes new crust (constructive).
Plates slide past each other; crust is neither made nor destroyed (conservative).
The sinking of a denser plate under a less dense one into the mantle.
The theory that the lithosphere is broken into plates that move over the asthenosphere.

en.text: At convergent (destructive) boundaries plates meet and the denser plate is subducted: ocean–continent gives volcanic mountains such as the Andes, ocean–ocean gives island arcs such as the Marianas, continent–continent gives fold mountains such as the Himalayas. At divergent (constructive) boundaries plates part and magma makes new crust: ocean ridges and rift valleys. At transform (conservative) boundaries plates slide past each other, causing earthquakes, as on the San Andreas Fault.

screens.title: Which plate sinks?
screens.ask: An oceanic plate (basalt) meets a continental plate (granite). Which one is forced down?
opts: The oceanic plate, because it is denser
The continental plate, because it is heavier
screens.after: Basalt oceanic crust is denser than granite continental crust, so it is subducted.

screens.title: Convergent (destructive) boundaries
paras: Plates move toward each other; the denser one is subducted and destroyed.
Ocean–continent: Nazca under South American Plate → volcanoes of the Andes.
Ocean–ocean: an arc of volcanic islands, such as the Mariana Islands.
Continent–continent: crust is squeezed and lifted, e.g. India meeting Asia → Himalayas.

screens.title: Divergent and transform boundaries
paras: Divergent (constructive): plates move apart; magma rises and makes new seafloor at ocean ridges (Mid-Atlantic). This is seafloor spreading.
On land, divergence makes rift valleys: the East African Rift. It may one day become an ocean.
Transform (conservative): plates slide past; crust is neither made nor destroyed; stick-slip earthquakes (San Andreas Fault).

en.text: Plate motion is driven by the earth's internal heat. Convection currents in the asthenosphere rise under ocean ridges, spread sideways under the plates and sink at subduction zones, dragging the brittle plates along. Figure 1.9 also shows ridge push, where hot raised lithosphere slides away from a ridge, and slab pull, where a sinking cold slab pulls the plate behind it.

screens.title: A pot of boiling water
screens.ask: In a pot of hot water, warm water rises in the middle and sinks at the sides. What earth process is like this?
screens.after: Hot mantle rock rises, spreads and sinks in slow convection cells that drag the plates.

screens.title: Convection drives the plates
paras: Plate tectonics is driven by the earth's internal energy.
Rocks conduct heat poorly, so heat moves by convection.
The asthenosphere is ductile and can flow.
Hot currents rise at ocean ridges; cool currents sink at subduction zones.
The plates on top are dragged along.
Figure 1.9 also names ridge push and slab pull.

screens.text: Where do hot convection currents rise?
screens.why: Rising currents bring magma up at ridges; cool currents sink at trenches.

opts: a cold sinking plate pulls the rest of the plate after it
hot rock pushes away from a ridge
screens.ans: a cold sinking plate pulls the rest of the plate after it
screens.why: At a trench the dense slab sinks and drags the plate. (Ridge push is the push away from a ridge.)

notes.text: The key-term list omits "Destructive", used in the text for convergent boundaries. The introduction says plates "transverse"; the standard term is transform (sliding past).
Unit outcomes mention triple junctions and retarding forces of plate motion; these pages do not cover them. Ridge push and slab pull appear only in Figure 1.9 (items marked added).
